items.definition: The main categories of network defined by their geographic size and purpose.
items.examples: A LAN in one office; a WAN linking offices across the country; a PAN connecting a phone to earbuds.
items.examTip: LAN = one site; WAN = wide area (e.g. the internet); SAN = storage; PAN = personal (Bluetooth range).
keyFacts: LAN — Local Area Network (one site)
WLAN — Wireless LAN
WAN — Wide Area Network (large/geographic)
SAN — Storage Area Network; PAN — Personal Area Network
The internet — the global WAN

items.definition: Networks restricted to particular users rather than the open internet.
items.examples: A company intranet for staff; an extranet giving suppliers limited access; a private cloud network.
items.examTip: Intranet = internal only; Extranet = extends to selected outsiders (e.g. partners/suppliers).
keyFacts: Intranet — private network for an organisation's staff
Extranet — controlled access for selected external partners
Cloud network — private networking over cloud infrastructure

items.definition: Combining wired and wireless technologies in one network, and the issues this raises.
items.examples: Wi-Fi access points connected to a wired Ethernet backbone; managing channels to avoid interference.
items.examTip: Issues fall into compatibility, admin (channels/IP) and technical (signal strength/interference).
keyFacts: Ethernet standards for wired and wireless (802 family)
Compatibility/interoperability issues (protocols, access points)
Admin issues (channels, IP addresses)
Technical issues (signal strength, interference)

items.definition: Logical and physical diagrams that show how a network is laid out, sometimes including port numbers or addresses.
items.examples: Completing a network diagram by adding a firewall between the router and the switch (sample paper Q1).
items.examTip: You may be asked to interpret OR amend a network diagram — practise adding devices like firewalls and labelling connections.
keyFacts: Logical diagrams show data flow; physical diagrams show real devices/cabling
May show specific port numbers or network addresses
Exam may ask you to complete/amend a diagram

items.definition: The qualities organisations need from a network, several of which relate to security.
items.examples: Designing for scalability and fault tolerance so the network copes with growth and failures.
items.examTip: Security-related requirements include security settings, reliability, fault tolerance and backup management.
keyFacts: Scalability, performance/response time, reliability
Software/hardware and file sharing/compatibility
Backup management, security settings, fault tolerance, communications

items.definition: The physical and logical arrangement of devices on a network.
items.examples: A star topology where every device connects to a central switch; a wireless mesh for resilient coverage.
items.examTip: Physical topology = the layout of cables/devices; logical topology = how data actually flows (bus/ring).
keyFacts: Physical: star, extended star, hierarchical, wireless mesh, ad-hoc (BYOD)
Logical: logical bus, logical ring
Star is common — failure of one cable doesn't down the whole network

items.definition: The model used to organise how devices share resources and responsibilities.
items.examples: A client/server network with central control; a peer-to-peer network sharing files directly.
items.examTip: Client/server = central control & security; peer-to-peer = no central server; thin client = processing on the server.
keyFacts: Peer-to-peer — devices share resources directly, no central server
Client/server — central server controls resources and security
Thin client — minimal local device, processing done on the server

items.definition: Running multiple virtual machines/environments on one physical host, improving security through isolation.
items.examples: Sandboxing a suspicious program in an isolated virtual machine; segmenting workloads.
items.examTip: Security benefit: isolation/sandboxing reduces the attack surface and contains threats.
keyFacts: Segmentation of systems
Isolation/sandboxing/containerisation
Reduced attack surface

items.definition: Security risks that come with relying on cloud services.
items.examples: A default-open access setting exposing storage; account hijacking; an insecure API to a cloud service.
items.examTip: Cloud risks: misconfiguration/default settings, provider reliance, API vulnerabilities, account hijacking.
keyFacts: Configuration issues / default access settings
Reliance on the service provider; data leaks/loss/theft
API vulnerabilities in the interface to cloud services
Account hijacking

items.definition: Allowing staff to use their own devices for work, which creates data-security and management issues.
items.examples: An employee's personal phone holding company emails; wiping company data when they leave.
items.examTip: BYOD blurs personal/organisational data — issues include password policy, privacy, wiping data, and patching.
keyFacts: Organisational data on a private device
Issues: password policy, privacy, data security on/off device
Patches/updates/compatibility; separating org vs personal apps
Wiping data when no longer required; auditing data movement

items.definition: Further modern trends: software-defined networking, storage area networks, IoT, and remote working — each with security implications.
items.examples: SDN centrally managing segmentation; a home worker needing a VPN on an insecure home Wi-Fi.
items.examTip: Remote working risks: shared home devices, insecure home Wi-Fi, reliance on third-party tools — needs VPN/encryption.
keyFacts: SDN — segmentation, remote management, automation, scalability
SAN — redundancy, scalability, access controls, encryption
IoT — API issues, default passwords, no patches, botnets, eavesdropping
Remote working — shared devices, home Wi-Fi security, need for VPN

items.definition: Devices used directly by people, with connectivity and processing, plus fixed networked devices.
items.examples: Smartphones, laptops, tablets, smartwatches; servers, workstations, NAS, networked printers.
items.examTip: Split into mobile devices and fixed networked devices (server, PC, printer, scanner, NAS).
keyFacts: Mobile: phone, laptop, tablet, console, smartwatch, camera, VR/AR
Fixed: server, PC/workstation, printer, scanner, NAS
Multi-functional devices combine several of these

items.definition: Hardware that connects devices and networks together and directs traffic.
items.examples: A managed switch segmenting traffic; a router joining networks; a gateway translating between protocols.
items.examTip: Switch (connects devices in a LAN), router (joins networks), gateway (translates protocols), bridge, repeater, AP, modem.
keyFacts: Switch (managed/unmanaged), router (wired/wireless), gateway
Bridge, repeater, access point, USB hub (active/passive)
Modem: DSL/copper, optical fibre, wireless

items.definition: The cabled and wireless media that carry network data.
items.examples: Ethernet (CAT6) cable; optical fibre; Wi-Fi; Bluetooth; Li-Fi.
items.examTip: Optical fibre = fast, secure, hard to tap. Wireless media (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/NFC) are easier to intercept.
keyFacts: Cable: Ethernet, USB (current + legacy)
Wireless: Wi-Fi (802.11), NFC, Bluetooth, cellular/5G
Optical fibre and Li-Fi

items.definition: The security risks of removable storage and external media.
items.examples: A lost USB stick exposing data; an external drive used to spread malware; data corruption over time.
items.examTip: External media risks: loss/theft, interception/copying, malware vector, lifespan/failure — mitigated by encryption and secure disposal.
keyFacts: Encryption and secure disposal of media
Loss/theft and interception/copying
Data loss/corruption and media lifespan/failure
Acts as a malware vector

items.definition: The operating systems, monitoring tools and applications that run on a network.
items.examples: A packet sniffer analysing traffic; an events/logs viewer; remote-access admin tools.
items.examTip: Monitoring tools (performance monitor, logs viewer, vulnerability scanner, packet sniffer) are key for spotting incidents — link to D2.
keyFacts: Network/device OS: GUI, CLI, web interface for configuration
Monitoring tools: performance monitor, logs viewer, vulnerability scanner, packet sniffer
Applications: remote working tools, database, document management, mapping tools

items.definition: The core suite of protocols used to transmit data across networks and the internet, organised as a four-layer model.
items.examples: TCP breaking a file into packets, IP addressing them, and TLS securing the connection.
items.examTip: TCP/IP uses a four-layer model; TLS adds security; packets have headers; error correction ensures delivery.
keyFacts: Four-layer model
Transport Layer Security (TLS) for secure connections
Data sent as packets with headers
Error correction

items.definition: Ports identify services/connections; packets are the units data is broken into for transmission.
items.examples: Port 443 for HTTPS; a TCP packet with header, payload and trailer.
items.examTip: Packet structure: header (addresses), payload (data), trailer/footer (error check). Know TCP vs UDP.
keyFacts: Hardware ports (switch) vs software/virtual IP ports
Packet parts: header, payload/body, trailer/footer
Packet types: TCP (reliable), IP, UDP (fast, no guarantee)

items.definition: Network Address Translation maps private internal addresses to public ones; addressing uses IPv4/IPv6 and reserved private ranges.
items.examples: A home router using NAT so many devices share one public IP; 192.168.x.x private addresses.
items.examTip: Know the private ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x), APIPA (169.254.x) and loopback 127.0.0.1.
keyFacts: NAT types: static, dynamic, Port Address Translation (PAT)
IPv4 and IPv6 address formats
RFC 1918 private ranges: 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x
APIPA 169.254.x (DHCP failure); 127.0.0.1 loopback

items.definition: Dividing a network into segments to control access and limit how far an attacker can spread.
items.examples: Putting guest Wi-Fi on a separate segment from staff systems (sample paper Q2).
items.examTip: Segmentation security benefits: limits access, restricts lateral movement, smaller attack surface, simpler damage control.
keyFacts: Uses hierarchy, trust relationships and access control
Limits access to devices, data and applications
Restricts lateral movement of an attacker/malware
Smaller attack surface and simpler damage control

items.definition: The devices used to build and configure networks securely.
items.examples: A firewall filtering traffic; a router directing packets; a WAP providing wireless access.
items.examTip: For 'secure internet access' the expected device is a FIREWALL (sample paper Q1ai).
keyFacts: Server, router, switch
Wireless Access Point (WAP)
Firewall, bridge, gateway

items.definition: The service that resolves human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
items.examples: Typing www.example.com and DNS returning its IP address so the browser can connect.
items.examTip: DNS resolution = name → IP. DNS can be attacked (spoofing/poisoning) — link to A1.2.4.
keyFacts: DNS resolution process (name to IP)
Reverse DNS resolution (IP to name)
DNS cache and IPv6 DNS

items.definition: Services that manage identities and verify users across a network.
items.examples: Active Directory managing user accounts; MFA at login; single sign-on across apps.
items.examTip: Authentication types: single-factor, two-factor (TFA), multi-factor (MFA), single sign-on (SSO). Protocols: PAP, CHAP, EAP.
keyFacts: Directory services: Active Directory, Open Directory, OpenLDAP
Authentication types: single-factor, TFA, MFA, SSO
Authentication protocols: PAP, CHAP, EAP

items.definition: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically assigns IP addresses and settings to devices on a network.
items.examples: A laptop joining Wi-Fi and being given an IP address, gateway and lease automatically.
items.examTip: DHCP config includes IP range, lease length, gateway, reservations. DHCP has no built-in security (sample paper Q3) — open to spoofing.
keyFacts: DHCP servers assign IPs to clients automatically
Config: address range, lease info, reservations, server address
Inherently insecure — no built-in security measures
Vulnerable to DHCP spoofing/rogue server attacks

items.definition: How data is routed between networks, and how remote users connect securely.
items.examples: A VPN giving a home worker secure access to office systems; BGP routing traffic across the internet.
items.examTip: A VPN creates an encrypted 'tunnel' over the internet so remote data can't be read if intercepted (sample paper Q2c).
keyFacts: Routing: static, dynamic/adaptive, routing tables
IGPs (within a network), EGPs/BGP (between networks/internet)
Remote access by dial-up or VPN over the internet
VPN encrypts the connection (a secure tunnel)

items.definition: Services that provide shared file storage and shared printing across a network.
items.examples: A file server holding shared documents; a print server queuing and prioritising print jobs.
items.examTip: File server = central storage; print server = manages shared printers, queues and drivers.
keyFacts: File server — networked file storage, tracking, sharing
Print server — sharing, queueing, prioritising
Printer configuration and driver management

items.definition: Services delivering web, email and real-time communication, several of which lack built-in encryption.
items.examples: A web server using HTTPS; email sent via SMTP; a VoIP call.
items.examTip: Mail protocols (SMTP, POP, MIME) lack built-in encryption — a security weakness. Web services use HTTP/HTTPS and XML.
keyFacts: Web services: HTTP/HTTPS, XML, OS/language independent
Mail services: SMTP, POP, MIME — lack built-in encryption
Comms: email, VoIP, SMS, video conferencing, CaaS
